subject: Business
title: Hedging: Protecting Against Downside
description: A 60-second lesson on Hedging: Protecting Against Downside.

hook.text: A farmer locks in wheat prices before harvest using a futures contract. If prices drop, they're protected.

buildup.text: Hedging means taking a financial position that offsets potential losses in another investment.

discovery.text: Options, futures, and inverse ETFs let investors protect portfolios without selling their holdings.

twist.text: Hedging has a cost — like insurance premiums. Over-hedging can eat into returns more than the losses it prevents.

climax.text: Airlines hedge fuel prices years in advance. Southwest saved $3.5 billion by hedging before oil prices spiked.

punchline.text: You can't eliminate risk. But you can choose which risks to keep and which to transfer.

quiz.question: What is financial hedging?
options: Taking a position that offsets potential losses in another investment
Investing only in safe government bonds

details.summary: Hedging uses financial instruments to offset potential losses in an investment or portfolio. Like buying insurance for your investments, strategies include options contracts, inverse funds, and diversification into negatively correlated assets to limit downside risk.
details.whyItMatters: Pure growth strategies leave portfolios exposed to devastating drawdowns. Hedging protects gains and limits losses during market downturns, helping investors stay invested through volatility rather than panic-selling.
takeaways: Hedging offsets potential losses using instruments that gain when markets fall
Put options give the right to sell at a set price, limiting downside exposure
Hedging has a cost that reduces overall returns during rising markets

faq.question: What is the simplest hedging strategy for individual investors?
faq.answer: Diversifying into bonds, which tend to rise when stocks fall, is the most accessible hedge. Treasury bonds specifically have historically provided strong protection during stock market crashes. This requires no options knowledge or complex instruments.

faq.question: Why don't all investors hedge their portfolios?
faq.answer: Hedging costs money through option premiums, reduces upside potential, and adds complexity. Over long time horizons, market declines are temporary, so the cost of continuous hedging often exceeds the losses it prevents. Most long-term investors rely on diversification instead.
